# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

On AWS, numbers about a system are CloudWatch metrics: values with a namespace, a name and dimensions, summarised per period with a statistic (Sum, Average, Maximum, p95). Applications can create their own metrics without any API call by printing a JSON log line in Embedded Metric Format (EMF); CloudWatch Logs extracts the metrics from it. A CloudWatch alarm watches one metric (or a metric-math expression) and moves between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT\_DATA; a composite alarm combines alarms into one signal; a dashboard puts the widgets of one audience on one page.  
In this lab you deploy a simulated shop that writes EMF metrics every minute, read one EMF log line, explore the metrics with statistics, metric math and Metrics Insights, create a rate-based alarm, a latency alarm and a composite alarm with an SNS topic, build a dashboard from a JSON template, and test it all with a fault switch. Everything is done in the AWS Management Console.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You get notified about a checkout problem within minutes, and by one notification instead of three. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You read the same numbers three ways — graph, Metrics Insights query and alarm history — and know which statistic to trust. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your alarms have a rate-based threshold, M-of-N datapoints and one owner, and your dashboard passes the five-second test. |

It runs healthy at about 1 % errors and p95 ≈ 270 ms. A Lambda environment variable FAULT switches on payment-errors (about 40 % failed orders) or payment-slow (p95 ≈ 1.6 s). |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

One Lambda log line becomes metrics, alarm states and dashboard widgets. The metric name and the dimensions connect them.  
*Figure: EMF to Dashboard — Lambda Prints {"\_aws": {…Namespace ShopLab/\<your name\>, Dimensions \[Service\]…}, Requests, Errors, LatencyMs\[ \]} → CloudWatch Logs Extracts Metrics → Alarm (Errors/Requests \> 5 %, 3 of 3\) → Composite Alarm → SNS; Dashboard Widgets Read the Same Metrics*

| Service | What It Holds | Query Tool | Typical Question |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| CloudWatch Metrics | Numbers per namespace, dimension and period | Metrics explorer · Metrics Insights · metric math | How many, how fast, what trend? |
| Embedded Metric Format | A JSON log line that CloudWatch turns into metrics | Logs → Metrics (no API call) | How do I publish business numbers cheaply? |
| CloudWatch alarm | State OK / ALARM / INSUFFICIENT\_DATA of a metric or expression | Alarms → History | When must someone act? |
| Composite alarm and dashboard | A rule over alarms; one page of widgets | Alarms → Composite · Dashboards | One notification, one page for on-call |

*Figure: Alarm Evaluation — One Datapoint per Period (1 min); Alarm Needs M Breaching Datapoints out of N (3 of 3); Metric Delay Plus 3 Periods Means About 4–5 Minutes From Fault to ALARM*

* Deploy a metric-emitting Lambda and read an Embedded Metric Format log line  
* Explore metrics with statistics, metric math and Metrics Insights  
* Create rate-based and latency alarms and combine them in a composite alarm  
* Build a CloudWatch dashboard from JSON and add an alarm-status widget  
* Test the alarms with a fault switch and read the alarm history  
* Explain statistic, period, datapoints to alarm and missing-data settings

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| ✗  NEVER run this lab in a production AWS account — use a sandbox |
| ✗  NEVER put personal data or secrets into log lines or metric dimensions |
| ✗  NEVER alarm on a single datapoint or on a raw error count — use a rate and M of N datapoints |
| ✗  NEVER send the same incident to the pager from three alarms — only the composite alarm notifies |
| ✗  NEVER leave the stack, alarms and dashboard behind — the schedule runs every minute until you delete the stack |

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Metrics, EMF and Statistics

CloudWatch stores a metric as datapoints: for each period (here 1 minute) one statistic over the values received. A Lambda function can create metrics without calling the CloudWatch API: it prints a JSON line with an "\_aws" block (namespace, dimensions, metric names and units) — Embedded Metric Format — and CloudWatch Logs extracts the metrics. A metric can carry an array of values (LatencyMs has 30 per minute), which makes percentile statistics such as p95 possible. Metrics usually appear 1–2 minutes after the log line.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| An alarm that fires on every blip trains people to ignore it. A rate-based alarm with M of N datapoints and one composite notification tells the truth: customers are affected now. |
|  |
| Metrics, alarms and dashboards are one chain: the metric must exist, the alarm must watch the right statistic, and the dashboard must show the same numbers the alarm uses — otherwise on-call argues about which graph is right. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Statistic, Period and Datapoints to Alarm

The statistic decides what you see: Average hides a slow minority, p95 shows what the slowest 5 % experience, Maximum shows the worst case, Sum counts events. The period is the length of one datapoint. An alarm uses "M out of N datapoints": 3 out of 3 one-minute datapoints must breach before it goes to ALARM, which filters single spikes but adds about three minutes of delay.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With Alarms |
| :---- |
| An engineer creates an alarm "Errors \> 0 for 1 datapoint". The shop normally has about 1 % failed orders, so the alarm fires several times a day. After a week everybody has muted it — and the real incident is missed. |
|  |
| REASON: The threshold was below the normal baseline, a count was used instead of a rate, and one datapoint is enough to alarm. |
|  |
| YOU MUST measure the baseline first, alarm on the error rate (Errors / Requests) with a threshold above it, and require M of N datapoints. |

## 3.3  Alarm Settings and Statistics You Need

| Setting | Meaning | Lab Value | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Statistic | Sum, Average, Maximum, p50/p95 | Errors: Sum · LatencyMs: p95 | Average hides the slow tail |
| Period | Length of one datapoint | 1 minute | Shorter periods cost more and are noisier |
| Datapoints to alarm | M breaching datapoints out of N | 3 out of 3 | Filters single spikes; adds delay |
| Missing data | What no data means for the alarm | Treat as missing | Keeps the state when the generator pauses |

| 📝  How to Decide What Deserves an Alarm |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Who acts on this alarm, and how fast?" If nobody acts, it is a dashboard widget, not an alarm. If someone must act within minutes, alarm on the symptom customers feel (error rate, latency) with a rate and M of N datapoints. Use causes (CPU, queue depth) as extra widgets or low-severity alarms, and combine alarms in a composite alarm so that one problem sends one notification. |

| Step 2: 6 rows (3 minutes × 2 services), Requests \= 30, Errors 0–1, fault \= none |
| Step 3: 6 metrics — Errors, LatencyMs, Requests for Service \= checkout and Service \= payment (they appear 2–3 minutes after the first line) |
| **1.A  Why did the function not need to call the CloudWatch API to create these metrics? Which parts of the "\_aws" block decide the namespace, the dimensions and the unit?**  Answer: The function only prints a JSON line. CloudWatch Logs recognises the "\_aws" block and creates the metrics from it: CloudWatchMetrics.Namespace gives the namespace (ShopLab/\<your name\>), Dimensions lists the dimension names (Service), and each entry of Metrics gives a metric name and Unit (Requests, Errors, LatencyMs). The values come from the properties with the same names; a value array such as LatencyMs holds 30 samples.   |

You graph requests and errors, compare the Average, p95 and Maximum statistics of the latency, calculate the error rate with metric math and read the same numbers with Metrics Insights queries. Use the Metrics page of the CloudWatch console only.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Statistics, metric math and Metrics Insights (Metrics page) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: CloudWatch → Metrics → All metrics → ShopLab/\<your name\> → Service → tick Requests and Errors of checkout → Graphed metrics: Statistic \= Sum, Period \= 1 minute → time range 1h ![][image19] |
|  ![][image20] \# Step 2: add LatencyMs of checkout three times (Graphed metrics → ⋮ → Duplicate): Statistic Average, p95 and Maximum; Period \= 1 minute — compare the three lines ![][image21] |
| ![][image22] \# Step 3: error rate with metric math — Add math ▾ → Start with empty expression, id e1, label "Error rate %": ![][image23] |
| 100 \* m1 / m2 ![][image24] |
|  \#   (m1 \= Errors Sum of checkout, m2 \= Requests Sum of checkout; untick m1 and m2 so that only e1 is drawn) ![][image25] |
| \# Step 4: Query tab → Editor (Metrics Insights), run each query: |
| SELECT SUM(Errors) FROM SCHEMA("ShopLab/u07", Service) GROUP BY Service ![][image26] |
|  SELECT MAX(LatencyMs) FROM SCHEMA("ShopLab/u07", Service) GROUP BY Service ORDER BY MAX() DESC  ![][image27] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: Requests \= 30 per minute · Errors 0 or 1 per minute (a few per hour) |
| Step 2: checkout LatencyMs — Average ≈ 210 ms · p95 ≈ 270 ms · Maximum ≈ 290–310 ms (payment is about 55 ms lower) |
| Step 3: error rate 0 % most minutes, 3.3 % when one order failed — never above 5 % |
| Step 4: Errors per Service: checkout and payment have the same sum (each failed order fails in both) · highest latency: checkout, then payment |
| **2.A  LatencyMs: Average ≈ 210 ms, p95 ≈ 270 ms, Maximum ≈ 300 ms. Which statistic would you use for an alarm, and why is the Average not enough?**  Answer: The p95: it shows what the slowest 5 % of customers see. In a partial slowdown the Average moves little while p95 and Maximum jump; the Maximum alone is too sensitive to single outliers. For this alarm I use p95 \> 800 ms.   |
| **2.B  Why is the error rate (Errors / Requests) a better alarm input than the Errors sum?**  Answer: A rate adapts to traffic: 3 errors in 30 orders is serious, 3 errors in 3 000 orders is not. A count would either fire at peak traffic or miss an incident at night. The rate also makes the threshold readable (5 %).   |

| \#   Name: shop-checkout-latency-p95-\<your name\> |
| \# Composite alarm — Alarms → Create composite alarm → Alarm rule (Editor): ![][image32] |
| ALARM("shop-checkout-error-rate-u07") OR ALARM("shop-checkout-latency-p95-u07") |
| \#   Notification: In alarm → Select an existing SNS topic → shop-alerts-\<your name\> → Name: shop-checkout-degraded-\<your name\> → Create composite alarm ![][image33] |

| **![][image34] 📟  Expected Output** |
| Alarms list: shop-checkout-error-rate-\<your name\> and shop-checkout-latency-p95-\<your name\> go from "Insufficient data" to OK within 3–4 minutes; shop-checkout-degraded-\<your name\> is OK |
| After the fault: about 12 of 30 orders fail per minute (≈ 40 %); the error-rate alarm needs 3 breaching minutes plus the metric delay — ALARM after about 4–5 minutes; the latency alarm stays OK |
| **3.A  Your error-rate alarm needs 3 out of 3 datapoints. How long after the fault starts will it reach ALARM, and what do you gain for that delay?**  Answer: About 4–5 minutes: up to 1 minute until the EMF metric is available, 3 minutes of breaching datapoints and up to 1 minute until the alarm is evaluated. In return one or two odd minutes cannot start an alarm; with 1 of 1 the alarm would fire on every single failed order and be muted within a week.   |
| **3.B  Why do the two child alarms have no notification and only the composite alarm has one?**  Answer: One incident usually breaks several symptoms at once (errors and latency). If every alarm notified, on-call would get several pages for one problem. The composite alarm turns them into one signal: it is in ALARM while any child is in ALARM and sends one notification; the child alarms stay visible in the dashboard and history for diagnosis.   |

That is acceptable for a rate alarm that must not page on blips; for a hard outage use a shorter rule (for example 2 of 2\) or an extra alarm on a stricter symptom.   |

| **V6: Did the alarms react to the fault?**  Answer: Yes — after about 4–5 minutes the error-rate alarm and the composite alarm went to ALARM; the history shows the reason.   |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Stack creation fails: "already exists" | Log group or function of an earlier attempt with the same your name | CloudFormation → Events tab of the failed stack | Delete the failed stack and the old log group /aws/lambda/shop-orders-\<your name\>; create again |
| No metrics in ShopLab/\<your name\> | Schedule has not run yet or the function failed | Lambda → shop-orders-\<your name\> → Monitor → Invocations | Wait 2–3 minutes; check the EventBridge rule is enabled and the log group has events |
| Alarm stays "Insufficient data" | Metric math has no data yet or the wrong dimension | Open the alarm → Details → graph | Wait 3 minutes; select Service \= checkout for both metrics |
| Alarm does not reach ALARM | Fault not saved or threshold/statistic wrong | Check environment variable FAULT and the alarm settings | Save FAULT \= payment-errors; error-rate threshold 5, 3 of 3, Sum, 1 minute |
| Dashboard: "Invalid JSON" | \_\_your name\_\_ or \_\_REGION\_\_ not replaced, or text cut during paste | Source editor shows the error line | Replace both placeholders everywhere; paste the whole file |
| Composite alarm cannot be created | Child alarm names in the rule are wrong | Alarms list: copy the exact names | Use the exact alarm names with your your name id |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — One Incident, One Notification |
| :---- |
| Why do the child alarms have no notification and the composite alarm has one? |
| What would on-call have received without the composite alarm? |
|  |
| Key insight: one problem should produce one page; child alarms stay as diagnostic signals. |
| **Discussion 2 — Three Ways to Make a Metric** |
| Compare EMF, PutMetricData and a log metric filter: where is the code, and what does each cost? |
| When would you choose EMF in a Lambda function? |
|  |
| Key answer: EMF needs only a log line (no API call, no extra latency); PutMetricData needs an SDK call; metric filters work on existing logs without code changes but cannot carry arrays. |
| **Discussion 3 — Compare With Log-Only Counting** |
| In Lab 1 the Errors metric showed 3 while 9 orders failed. How would an EMF Errors metric from the function have shown 9? |
| Which alarm would you build on it? |
|  |
| Answer: the function counts every failed order (timeouts and declines) in the Errors property of an EMF line; alarm on Errors/Requests as in this lab. |
| **Discussion 4 — From Dashboard to Runbook** |
| What is missing on your dashboard before 3 a.m. on-call can act on it? |
| Which widget do you look at first? |
|  |
| Key answer: a link to the runbook, the owner, a description of the audience and the alarm-status widget in the first row. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Alarm on one datapoint | Easy to create | Fires on every blip, then is muted | M of N datapoints (3 of 3\) |
| Alarm on a raw count | Count is the default metric | Fires at peak, silent at night | Alarm on a rate (Errors / Requests) |
| Looking at Average only | Default statistic | Slow tail invisible | Use p95 for latency |
| Every alarm notifies | Simple setup | Several pages per incident | Composite alarm notifies once |
| Leaving the stack | Forgot clean-up | Cost every minute (schedule) | Delete stack, alarms, dashboard |

# 8\. EXTENSION TASKS (Advanced Learners)

| Extension A — Latency Fault |
| :---- |
| Set FAULT \= payment-slow and wait for shop-checkout-latency-p95-\<your name\> and the composite alarm. |
| Compare the time to ALARM with the error-rate alarm — which is faster, and why? |
| Key question: is 800 ms the right threshold for p95? Update Lambda function `shop-orders-u07` (`eu-west-1`) environment variable `FAULT` to `payment-slow` and note the timestamp. Both alarms use `3 out of 3` 1-minute datapoints (\~4–5 minutes total with metric delivery/evaluation delay), so timing is similar when starting from `OK`; if `shop-checkout-degraded-u07` is already `ALARM` from an earlier error-rate breach, it stays `ALARM` while `shop-checkout-latency-p95-u07` transitions `OK` → `ALARM`. **Is `800 ms` the right p95 threshold?** Against a \~`270 ms` normal `p95` baseline, `800 ms` is \~3× higher and can miss moderate slowdowns (such as \~450–650 ms) that already degrade user experience; a tighter threshold (e.g., \~`450–500 ms`) or an additional warning threshold is often more practical depending on SLOs.  |
| **Extension B — Anomaly Detection** |
| Add an anomaly detection band to the Requests metric (Graphed metrics → Add anomaly detection) and an alarm on it. |
| Set FAULT \= payment-slow and look at Requests: does the band catch a change that a static threshold would miss? |
| Extension C — Cost and Quotas Add an anomaly detection band to `Requests` (`ShopLab/u07` → `Service` → `checkout`) in CloudWatch Metrics and create an alarm on it. Unlike a static threshold on latency/error value, an anomaly band models historical trends/seasonality and can catch unusual shifts or drops/spikes in `Requests` volume during `FAULT = payment-slow` that a fixed static number would miss.  |
| **Open Billing → Cost Explorer (or the instructor's cost sheet): which items of this lab cost money?** |
| What would 100 such stacks cost for a month, and how do you prevent that? |
| Which quota (concurrent executions, alarms, dashboards) limits a cohort of 40? |
| Which fields would it set for correlation?  **Cost drivers:** CloudWatch custom metrics, alarms/composite alarms/anomaly alarms, dashboards, CloudWatch Logs ingestion/storage, Lambda invocations/duration, and SNS notifications. **100 stacks for a month & prevention:** Multiplying custom metrics, alarms, dashboards, logs, and Lambda runs by 100 across \~30 days scales monthly charges substantially—prevent this by deleting stacks/alarms/dashboards right after lab validation, keeping short log/metric retention, avoiding unnecessary custom metrics, and using billing alerts/cleanup automation. **40-seat cohort quota limits:** Watch **CloudWatch Alarms**, **CloudWatch Dashboards**, and **Lambda Concurrent Executions** in `eu-west-1` (40 concurrent students running tests can hit account/region concurrency or resource limits if shared/unmonitored). **Correlation fields:** Typically `correlationId` / `requestId` / `traceId`, `service` (`checkout`, `payment`), `fault` (`none`, `payment-errors`, `payment-slow`), `seat` (`u07`), and `timestamp`.  |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — CLOUDWATCH METRICS, ALARMS & DASHBOARD CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Metric (EMF) | {"\_aws":{"CloudWatchMetrics":\[{"Namespace":…,"Dimensions":\[\["Service"\]\],"Metrics":\[…\]}\]}, …} | Custom metric from a log line |
| Statistics | Sum · Average · Maximum · p95 | Per period |
| Metric math | 100 \* m1 / m2 | Error rate |
| Metrics Insights | SELECT SUM(Errors) FROM SCHEMA("ShopLab/u07", Service) GROUP BY Service | SQL over metrics |
| Alarm settings | Threshold · period · M of N datapoints · missing data | Alarm design |
| Alarm states | OK · ALARM · INSUFFICIENT\_DATA | Alarm history |
| Composite alarm | ALARM("a") OR ALARM("b") | One signal |
| SNS topic | shop-alerts-\<your name\> | Notification |
| Dashboard source | Dashboards → Actions → View/edit source | JSON |
| Fault switch | Lambda → Configuration → Environment variables → FAULT | none · payment-errors · payment-slow |
| Baseline | Healthy: ≈ 1 % errors · checkout p95 ≈ 270 ms | Thresholds from data |
| Clean-up | Stack · 3 alarms · dashboard | Always |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — nothing in this lab needs a command line for the learners; the instructor prepares the account once.  
1\. Account and region: one sandbox AWS account (never production) and one region for the cohort. Learners need the sandbox policy in the kit (aws/instructor/learner-sandbox-policy.json) or equivalent rights for CloudFormation, Lambda, EventBridge, SNS, CloudWatch alarms and dashboards. Review the policy in your account before class; it has not been tested in your organisation.  
2\. Template check (once, before class): create the stack with your name u00, wait 3 minutes, check the metrics, run the expected statistics (Requests 30; Errors 0–1; checkout p95 ≈ 270 ms), set FAULT \= payment-errors and confirm ALARM after 4–5 minutes with your own alarms, then delete everything. Alarm timing depends on how fast EMF metrics are published in your region — adjust the expected 4–5 minutes in the guide if it differs.  
3\. Quotas: 40 learners × (1 Lambda, 1 EventBridge rule, 3 alarms, 1 dashboard, 6 custom metrics). The defaults of CloudWatch (alarms, dashboards, custom metrics), EventBridge rules and SNS topics are far above this; check Lambda concurrent executions (one invocation per learner per minute, negligible).  
4\. Notifications: the AlertEmail parameter creates an e-mail subscription that each learner must confirm; leave it empty if learners should not receive e-mail — the composite alarm still changes state and the SNS topic still exists. Do not use a shared mailbox for 40 learners.  
5\. Cost control: the schedule invokes the generator every minute (about 43 000 invocations per month per stack). After class delete the stacks (search CloudFormation for shop-lab2-\*), then the alarms (shop-checkout-\*) and dashboards (shop-checkout-\*) that learners created by hand — CloudFormation does not remove them. Custom metrics expire by themselves after 15 months but are billed meanwhile.  
6\. No CloudFormation access? Learners create the Lambda function by hand (Python 3.13, paste shop-orders-generator.py, environment variables NAMESPACE \= ShopLab/\<your name\> and FAULT \= none, timeout 10 s), an EventBridge rule rate(1 minute) targeting it, and an SNS topic. Allow 15 more minutes.
